title: What Percentage of Your Life Outcomes Do You Control
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece introduces psychologist Julian Rotter's concept of locus of control and explores how it shapes workplace performance and culture fit. People with an internal locus of control attribute outcomes to their own effort and tend to show higher job satisfaction, lower stress, and more initiative around feedback and skill-building. Those with an external locus of control attribute outcomes to luck or authority, and tend to be more comfortable with supervision, more adaptable to change, and less risk-averse. The essay suggests organizations can and do use this distinction deliberately in hiring, matching belief style to role and culture.
points: Julian Rotter's 1950s concept of locus of control distinguishes people who attribute outcomes to their own effort (internal) from those who attribute them to luck or authority (external).
Internals report higher job satisfaction, lower stress and attrition, and are more likely to seek out and act on feedback.
Externals are more comfortable with direct supervision, collaborate well with peers, and adapt more readily to change.
Externals tend to be less risk-averse than internals because they don't believe outcomes are fully within their control.
Some organizations deliberately use locus-of-control assessments as part of hiring to match belief style to role and culture.
quotes: What we believe about the rewards and punishments in life and where they come from exerts an enormous influence on how we orient to the world.
Those who see life and its assorted outcomes as a function of their hard work, skill, and perseverance possess an internal locus of control.
Those with an internal locus of control consistently report higher job satisfaction, lower stress, and lower attrition.
Externals tend to be more satisfied with direct supervision, collaborate more successfully with peers, and are more motivated by rewards other than financial incentives.
Given the goals, culture and tasks of any particular organization, it may be beneficial to select talent with more of one belief set than the other.
